extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO officials, judges, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Legislative amendments and procedural standards for patent prosecution, post-grant proceedings, venue, inequitable conduct, micro-entity status, PTAB composition and duties, and related administrative rules. Covers definitions, submission requirements, standards of proof, timing, and regulatory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'cancellation petitioner'
rubrics_metrics.description: “The term ‘cancellation petitioner’ means the real party in interest requesting cancellation of any claim of a patent under chapter 32 of this title and the privies of the real party in interest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies who may be treated as the petitioner in post-grant cancellation proceedings—the real party in interest and its privies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Trial and Appeal Board: establishment and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: “There shall be in the Office a Patent Trial and Appeal Board. The Director, the Deputy Director, the Commissioner for Patents, the Commissioner for Trademarks, and the administrative patent judges shall constitute the Patent Trial and Appeal Board. The administrative patent judges shall be persons of competent legal knowledge and scientific ability who are appointed by the Director.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies which officers and judges constitute the PTAB and qualification/appointment standard for administrative patent judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB duties and panel composition
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Patent Trial and Appeal Board shall— (1) on written appeal of an applicant, review adverse decisions of examiners upon application for patents; (2) on written appeal of a patent owner, review adverse decisions of examiners upon patents in reexamination proceedings under chapter 30; (3) review appeals by patent owners and third-party requesters under section 315; (4) determine priority and patentability of invention in derivation proceedings under section 135(a); and (5) conduct post-grant opposition proceedings under chapter 32.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each appeal and derivation proceeding shall be heard by at least 3 members designated by the Director; only the PTAB may grant rehearings; Director assigns each post-grant review proceeding to a panel of 3 APJs who have responsibilities under chapter 32.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preissuance submissions by third parties — timing
rubrics_metrics.description: “Any person may submit ... any patent, published patent application, or other publication of potential relevance ... if such submission is made in writing before the earlier of— (A) the date a notice of allowance under section 151 is mailed in the application for patent; or (B) either— (i) 6 months after the date on which the application for patent is published under section 122, or (ii) the date of the first rejection under section 132 of any claim by the examiner during the examination of the application for patent, whichever occurs later.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the deadline window for third-party prior-art submissions: before notice of allowance, but subject to the 6-month-after-publication / date-of-first-rejection cutoff (whichever is later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preissuance submissions — required content
rubrics_metrics.description: “Any submission under paragraph (1) shall— (A) set forth a concise description of the asserted relevance of each submitted document; (B) be accompanied by such fee as the Director may prescribe; and (C) include a statement by the submitter affirming that the submission was made in compliance with this section.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party submissions must include a concise relevance statement for each document, the prescribed fee, and a certification of compliance; Director may set fee amount and other requirements by regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpatentable subject matter: tax planning methods
rubrics_metrics.description: “A patent may not be obtained for a tax planning method.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express statutory exclusion: methods, plans, strategies, or schemes designed to reduce/minimize/defer tax liability are not patentable subject matter under amended section 101(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'tax planning method'
rubrics_metrics.description: “the term ‘tax planning method’ means a plan, strategy, technique, or scheme that is designed to reduce, minimize, or defer, or has, when implemented, the effect of reducing, minimizing, or deferring, a taxpayer’s tax liability, but does not include the use of tax preparation software or other tools used solely to perform or model mathematical calculations or prepare tax or information returns;”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes disallowed tax-planning patents from permitted software tools limited to calculations or return preparation/modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of 'taxpayer', 'tax', 'State' for section 101(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the term ‘taxpayer’ means an individual, entity, or other person ...; the terms ‘tax’, ‘tax laws’, ‘tax liability’, and ‘taxation’ refer to any Federal, State, county, city, municipality, or other governmental levy ...; and the term ‘State’ means each of the several States, the District of Columbia, and any commonwealth, territory, or possession of the United States.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies scope of tax-related terms to include federal, state, and local levies and the range of persons covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue prohibition on manufactured venue
rubrics_metrics.description: “Notwithstanding section 1391 of this title, in any civil action arising under any Act of Congress relating to patents, a party shall not manufacture venue by assignment, incorporation, or otherwise to invoke the venue of a specific district court.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents parties (e.g., plaintiffs) from manipulating corporate form or assignments to create favorable venue in a particular district.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible venues for patent infringement and declaratory judgment actions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Any civil action for patent infringement or any action for declaratory judgment may be brought only in a judicial district— (1) where the defendant has its principal place of business or in the location or place in which the defendant is incorporated ...; (2) where the defendant has committed a substantial portion of the acts of infringement and has a regular and established physical facility that the defendant controls ...; (3) where the primary plaintiff resides, if the primary plaintiff ... is an institution of higher education ...; or (4) where the plaintiff resides, if the plaintiff or a subsidiary ... has an established physical facility in such district dedicated to research, development, or manufacturing ... or if the sole plaintiff ... is an individual inventor who ... qualifies ... as a micro entity ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates district-specific bases for venue, including principal place of business/incorporation, substantial acts with a regular physical facility, and special rules for institutions of higher education, nonprofit organizations, plaintiffs with R&D/manufacturing facilities, and qualifying individual inventors; later expanded text includes additional categories (e.g., foreign-defendant cases, nonprofit plaintiffs, plaintiffs who are named inventors and have not assigned rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: District court transfer authority for patent venue
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the plaintiff brings a civil action for patent infringement in a judicial district under subsection (c), the district court may transfer that action to any other district or division where— (1) the defendant has substantial evidence or witnesses; and (2) venue would be appropriate under section 1391 of this title, if such transfer would be appropriate under section 1404 of this title.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows courts to transfer improperly or inconveniently venued actions when defendant evidence/witnesses are in another district and transfer satisfies 1404 considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory appeals of claim construction in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Adds interlocutory appealability: “(3) of an appeal from an interlocutory order or decree determining construction of claims in a civil action for patent infringement under section 271 of title 35. Application for an appeal under paragraph (3) shall be made to the court within 10 days after entry of the order or decree. The district court shall have discretion whether to approve the application and, if so, whether to stay proceedings in the district court during pendency of the appeal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates expedited interlocutory appeal path for claim construction orders, with a 10-day application window and district court discretion to permit the appeal and stay proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant disclosure requirement: search report and other information
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Director shall, by regulation, require that applicants submit a search report and other information and analysis relevant to patentability. An application shall be regarded as abandoned if the applicant fails to submit the required search report, information, and analysis in the manner and within the time period prescribed by the Director.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandates that the Director establish rules requiring applicants to provide prior-art search reports and relevant analysis, with failure-to-comply consequences (abandonment); micro-entity exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro-entity status — unassigned application certification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For an unassigned application, each inventor must certify that the inventor— (1) qualifies as a small entity as defined in regulations; (2) has not been named on five or more previously filed patent applications; (3) has not assigned, granted, or conveyed, and is not under an obligation to assign, grant, or convey, a license or any other ownership interest in the application; and (4) does not have a gross income exceeding 2.5 times the median household income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets objective eligibility criteria for micro-entity discounts/exceptions; income threshold tied to Bureau of the Census median household income; small-entity qualification per Director's regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro-entity status — assigned application certification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For an assigned application, each inventor must certify that the inventor— (1) qualifies as a small entity as defined in regulations and meets the income requirement; (2) has not been named on five or more previously filed patent applications; and (3) has assigned, granted, conveyed, or is under an obligation to assign, grant, or convey, a license or other ownership interest in the application to an entity that has five or fewer employees and has gross taxable income not exceeding 2.5 times the median household income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate micro-entity path when rights are assigned to small employers: ties eligibility to assignee size and income limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct defense — elements and standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: “A patent may be held to be unenforceable ... for inequitable conduct only if it is established, by clear and convincing evidence, that— (A) the patentee, its agents, or another person with a duty of disclosure to the Office, with the intent to mislead or deceive the patent examiner, misrepresented or failed to disclose material information concerning a matter or proceeding before the Office; and (B) in the absence of such deception, the Office, acting reasonably, would, on the record before it, have made a prima facie finding of unpatentability.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires both material misrepresentation/omission and intent to deceive, proven by clear and convincing evidence; materiality includes a but-for/prima facie unpatentability standard (see separate materiality criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct — intent requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: “In order to prove intent to mislead or deceive ... specific facts beyond materiality of the information submitted or not disclosed must be proven that support an inference of intent to mislead or deceive the Patent and Trademark Office. Facts support an inference of intent if they show circumstances that indicate conscious or deliberate behavior ... to not disclose material information or to submit materially false information.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materiality alone is insufficient to prove intent; plaintiff must plead/prove specific facts supporting an inference of conscious or deliberate deceptive behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct — defined remedies and referral for misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: “Upon a finding of inequitable conduct, the court shall balance the equities to determine which of the following remedies to impose: (A) Denying equitable relief to the patent holder and limiting the remedy for infringement to damages. (B) Holding the claims-in-suit, or the claims in which inequitable conduct occurred, unenforceable. (C) Holding the patent unenforceable. (D) Holding the claims of a related patent unenforceable. ... if there is evidence that the conduct can be attributable to a person or persons authorized to practice before the Office, the court shall refer the matter to the Office for appropriate disciplinary action under section 32, and shall order the parties to preserve and make available to the Office any materials that may be relevant to the determination under section 32.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a non-exhaustive list of possible equitable remedies and mandates referral to PTO disciplinary process when attorney/practitioner misconduct is implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading standard for inequitable conduct allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: “In an action involving any allegation of inequitable conduct under subsection (c), the party asserting this defense or claim shall comply with the pleading requirements set forth in Rule 9(b) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires fraud-type allegations (inequitable conduct) to meet Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirements in pleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode not a basis for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 282(b) amended: invalidity for failure to comply with section 112 excludes “the requirement that the specification shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removes best-mode disclosure as a standalone basis for invalidity or patent unenforceability in litigation—other section 112 requirements remain enforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO regulatory authority to ensure application quality and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: “The powers granted under paragraph (2) of subsection include the authority to promulgate regulations to ensure the quality and timeliness of applications and their examination, including specifying circumstances under which an application for patent may claim the benefit under sections 120, 121 and 365(c) of the filing date of a prior filed application for patent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorizes the PTO/Director to issue regulations focused on examination quality, timeliness, and rules governing priority/benefit claims under relevant sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation proceedings — settlement and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Parties to a derivation proceeding may terminate the proceeding by filing a written statement reflecting the agreement of the parties as to the correct inventors ... Unless the Patent Trial and Appeal Board finds the agreement to be inconsistent with the evidence of record, it shall take action consistent with the agreement. Any written settlement ... shall be filed with the Director. At the request of a party to the proceeding, the agreement or understanding shall be treated as business confidential information ... and shall be made available only to Government agencies on written request, or to any person on a showing of good cause.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits private settlement of derivation proceedings and allows confidentiality protections for settlement terms, subject to PTAB review for consistency with the record and exceptions on showing of good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation proceedings — arbitration option
rubrics_metrics.description: “Parties to a derivation proceeding, within such time as may be specified by the Director by regulation, may determine such contest or any aspect thereof by arbitration. Such arbitration shall be governed by the provisions of title 9 to the extent such title is not inconsistent with this section. The parties shall give notice of any arbitration award to the Director, and such award shall, as between the parties to the arbitration, be dispositive of the issues to which it relates. The arbitration award shall be unenforceable until such notice is given. Nothing in this subsection shall preclude the Director from determining patentability of the invention involved in the derivation proceeding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows arbitration to resolve inventorship disputes between parties if they choose, but the Director retains authority to determine patentability; arbitration awards must be notified to the Director to be enforceable between parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant review — effect of commencement
rubrics_metrics.description: “The commencement of a post-grant review proceeding— (1) shall not limit in any way the right of the patent owner to commence an action for infringement of the patent; and (2) shall not be cited as evidence relating to the validity of any claim of the patent in any proceeding before a court or the International Trade Commission concerning the patent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insulates patent owner’s infringement enforcement rights and prevents use of post-grant review commencement as evidentiary proof of invalidity in court/ITC proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to assert invalidity in ITC proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Adds that a party may “assert the invalidity of any such claim in defense to an action brought under section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1337).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that invalidity claims may be asserted as defenses in ITC Section 337 proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation petitions — required showing and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “for each claim sought to be canceled, the petition sets forth in writing the basis for cancellation and provides the evidence in support thereof, including copies of patents and printed publications, or written testimony of a witness attested to under oath or declaration by the witness, or any other information that the Director may require by regulation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes the substance of a cancellation petition: written basis and evidentiary support (documents, testimony under oath, or other Director-required information); later notes Director should consider that discovery must be in the interests of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director consideration of discovery in cancellation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: “In carrying out paragraph (3), the Director shall bear in mind that discovery must be in the interests of justice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directs the Director to weigh discovery requests against the interests of justice when overseeing post-grant cancellation proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of real party-in-interest in submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment adds requirement to “identify the real party-in-interest making the submission.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party submissions and related filings must identify the actual real party-in-interest submitting the information to the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search performance nationality/organizational requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the Director requires a search report to be submitted by applicants, and an applicant does not itself perform the search, the search must be performed by one or more individuals who are United States citizens or by a commercial entity that is organized under the laws of the United States or any State and employs United States citizens to perform such searches.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant delegates required search, the statute requires searches be performed by US citizens or US-organized entities employing US citizens (nationality/organizational requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant search report cannot substitute examiner search
rubrics_metrics.description: “Any search report required by the Director may not substitute in any way for a search by an examiner of the prior art during examination.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant-provided search reports are supplemental and do not relieve or replace the USPTO examiner's independent prior-art search responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct — materiality definition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Information is material under this section if— (A) In general.— (i) a reasonable examiner would have made a prima facie finding of unpatentability, or maintained a finding of unpatentability, of one or more of the patent claims based on the information, and the information is not cumulative to information already of record or previously considered by the Office; or (ii) information that is otherwise material refutes or is inconsistent with a position the applicant takes in opposing a rejection of the claim or in asserting an argument of patentability.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materiality requires that the information be non-cumulative and such that a reasonable examiner would have made (or maintained) a prima facie finding of unpatentability; alternatively, materiality may be shown if the information contradicts arguments or positions asserted by the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie finding standard for materiality
rubrics_metrics.description: “A prima facie finding of unpatentability under this section is shown if a reasonable examiner, based on a preponderance of the evidence, would conclude that the claim is unpatentable based on the information misrepresented or not disclosed, when that information is considered alone or in conjunction with other information or record. In determining whether there is a prima facie finding of unpatentability, each term in the claim shall be given its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and rebuttal evidence shall not be considered.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the evaluative lens for materiality: preponderance standard, broadest reasonable claim construction, and exclusion of rebuttal evidence when determining prima facie unpatentability for materiality purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study/report requirements on reexamination and special masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Directs the Under Secretary/Director and Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts to conduct studies and submit reports on the effectiveness/efficiency of reexamination proceedings and use of special masters, including enumerated factors to consider (frequency, role/powers, subject matter, impact on time/costs, training/experience, impact on reversal rate, and other helpful factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandates empirical/analytical reporting to Congress on specific topics, enumerating factors that should be included in assessments of reexamination procedures and special masters in patent litigation.
